answer:
Yes. ECE 201 (Circuits I) requires EF 152 or EF 158 with a grade of C or better, plus MATH 142 or MATH 148 with a grade of C or better [2].

A few other conditions apply:
- MATH 231 is a corequisite, so you can take it at the same time [2].
- The course is for electrical engineering and computer engineering students only and requires consent of the associate department head [2].
- PHYS 231 appears in the same term as ECE 201 in the Electrical Engineering plan, but it is not listed as a prerequisite for ECE 201 [1][2].
- The Electrical Engineering plan lists PHYS 136 and PHYS 138 as alternatives to EF 152 and EF 158 for a milestone [3], but the ECE 201 prerequisite names only EF 152 or EF 158 [2]. The catalog doesn't say whether the PHYS courses satisfy it, so check with your advisor if that's your route.

answer:
In these excerpts, only ECE 356 - Computer Systems Architecture (3 credit hours) names microcontrollers explicitly. It covers the architecture and design of microcomputer systems "with microprocessors or microcontrollers," including instruction set architectures, processor structures, memory hierarchy, and interfacing [1]. Its prerequisite is ECE 256 or COSC 230 with a grade of C or better [1].

Two other courses cover closely related topics, but their descriptions don't use the word "microcontroller":

- ECE 256 - Computer System Interfaces (3 credit hours) covers memory and I/O devices, timers, interrupts, direct memory access, and real-time operating system concepts, with hands-on lab work on a development system [4]. The prerequisite is ECE 255 with a grade of C or better [4].
- ECE 455 - Embedded Systems Design (3 credit hours) covers embedded systems for data acquisition and special-purpose computing, real-time software, and real-time operating systems [5]. The prerequisite is ECE 256 with a grade of C or better [5].

These excerpts may not include every ECE course, so other courses could also cover microcontrollers.

answer:
AI 201 (AI, Ethics, and Legal Frameworks, 3 credit hours) covers where artificial intelligence, ethics, and law meet [1]. According to the course description, you will:

- Explore the ethical challenges raised by emerging AI technologies and the societal effects of AI decisions [1]
- Study ethical principles central to AI design and deployment [1]
- Address bias, fairness, and transparency in AI systems [1]
- Discuss privacy and data rights [1]
- Look at global legal frameworks and regulation that govern AI, with insight into AI governance [1]

The goal is to prepare you to approach AI solutions with both their ethical and legal dimensions in mind [1].

The prerequisite is AI 101* or AI 102* or AI 111 [1]. The course is one of the elective options for the Applied Artificial Intelligence Certificate [2]. It is also listed in Term 3 of the BS in Applied Artificial Intelligence for the Technical Communication and Leadership Studies concentrations [4][5].

The catalog describes only course content. It doesn't cover assignments, workload, or how the class is taught day to day.

answer:
Several catalog courses cover machine learning. The main one is **COSC 325 - Introduction to Machine Learning**:

- **COSC 325 - Introduction to Machine Learning** (3 credit hours) covers clustering, decision trees, neural networks, statistical and Bayesian learning, dimension reduction, kernel methods, and reinforcement learning, with programming assignments [1].
  - Prerequisites: ECE 313 or ECE 317 or MATH 323 with a grade of C or better; and MATH 251 or MATH 257 with a grade of C or better. Prior knowledge may satisfy the prerequisite with consent of instructor [1].
- **COSC 322 - Tools for Applied Machine Learning** (3 credit hours) covers ML techniques for practical applications: data preprocessing, training, classification and prediction, and evaluation [4].
  - It may not be applied toward the computer science or computer engineering majors [4].
  - Prerequisites: COSC 101 or COSC 102 [Inactive] or COSC 111* or EF 230. Prior knowledge may satisfy the prerequisites with consent of instructor [4].
- **COSC 429 - Special Topics in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning** (3 credit hours) covers advanced topics. It may be repeated on a different topic, up to 6 hours maximum [3].
  - Prerequisite: COSC 325 with a grade of C or better [3].

Two other courses include machine learning as one topic among others:

- **COSC 423 - Introduction to Artificial Intelligence** [5]
- **ECE 476 - Introduction to Robotics**, which covers basic machine learning methods for adaptive behavior [2]

answer:
The excerpts don't directly say whether DATA 111 is meant for students with no coding experience, but here is what they do say.

- **DATA 111 - Data Knowledge and Discovery for Majors (3 credit hours)** "introduces students to programming through hands-on activities" and lists no prerequisite [5]. It does have a corequisite, CECS 250, and registration is restricted to CECS Data Science Majors [5]. If you're not in that major, you can't register for it.
- **DATA 101** exists, since the catalog says you can't receive credit for both DATA 101 and DATA 111 [5]. However, the excerpts don't describe DATA 101, so I can't tell you its prerequisites or whether it suits beginners.

If you specifically want a course for people new to programming, **COSC 111 - Computational Thinking and the Art of Programming (3 credit hours)** explicitly "welcomes students with limited or no programming experience" and satisfies the Volunteer Core (QR) requirement [3]. **AI 101 - Introduction to the World of AI (3 credit hours)** uses no-code AI platforms and satisfies Volunteer Core (EI) (QR) [1], but it's an AI course, not a DATA course.
